subject: Copywriting
title: Rewrite, Rewrite, Rewrite
description: A 60-second lesson on Rewrite, Rewrite, Rewrite.

hook.text: Gary Halbert wrote every sales letter at least 7 times. Ogilvy wrote 104 headlines for a single Rolls-Royce ad.

buildup.text: The first draft captures ideas. The second draft organizes them. The third through seventh drafts cut and sharpen.

discovery.text: Professional copywriters spend 20% of time writing and 80% rewriting. The polish is where the money lives.

twist.text: AI can generate first drafts instantly.

climax.text: Every legendary sales letter was rewritten until every word earned its place. If a word doesn't sell, it goes.

punchline.text: 104 headlines for one ad. Rewriting is the skill that pays.

quiz.question: How many headlines did Ogilvy write for his Rolls-Royce ad?

details.summary: The best sales letters are never written — they're rewritten. Gary Halbert wrote 20 to 30 drafts. Eugene Schwartz let copy sit for days between revisions. The rewriting process — cutting, tightening, and refining — transforms decent copy into million-dollar copy.
details.whyItMatters: Rewriting is where amateur copywriters separate from professionals. Understanding that first drafts are raw material — not finished products — changes the entire approach to writing and dramatically improves results.
takeaways: First drafts are for getting ideas down; revision is for making them great
Cutting words almost always improves copy — most first drafts are 30% too long
Distance between writing and editing sessions improves revision quality

faq.question: How many times should you rewrite?
faq.answer: Until every word earns its place and nothing can be removed without weakening the piece. Most professionals rewrite at least 5 to 10 times. Read aloud, cut anything that sounds like filler, and test multiple versions. If you're not embarrassed by your first draft, you're not improving enough.

faq.question: What should you focus on during revision?
faq.answer: First pass: Does the structure and flow work? Second pass: Is every claim supported by proof? Third pass: Can any word, sentence, or paragraph be cut without loss? Fourth pass: Read aloud — does it sound natural? Final pass: Is the CTA clear and compelling?
